utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the basis of this document that we see here, I really do not understand how the distinguished witness can make any kind of conclusion. There is a -- this is a document that mentions a particular person with a certain name and surname. As far as I understand things, the witness never saw this document expect perhaps during the proofing before his testimony. I really wonder how, on the basis of a name and surname that is very common in Serbia, this witness can conclude who this actually is. With all due respect to the distinguished witness, I really think that he cannot do more than speculate as far as this document is concerned. Perhaps we will discuss other aspects of this document later, when we discuss it once it is perhaps being tendered into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, what's your objection against the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my objection is twofold. First of all, the witness is being asked to speculate and it is this line of questioning that leads to speculation, guess-work, that is the first objection. And also, indirectly through these question what is sought is admission into evidence on the basis of this speculation. So there are two troublesome aspects to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Whether the witness is speculating or not and whether that should affect our decision on admission is still to be seen. At the same time, Ms. Marcus, if you could further explore how common the name is and what other -- apart from approximately the same age -- there may be other matters in this document which would -- which would give a -- a solid factual basis for any conclusions you asked the witness to draw from this document. Because, although it is a mixed matter, fact, and whether it's the same person, we should know exactly what the factual basis for it is, and where it is just making that last step and saying it's the same person. Could you please further explore that. By the way, Mr. Petrovic, it is it matter which you could have thoroughly explored in cross-examination as well. And to say that the witness is asked to speculate is certainly too strong. Ms. Marcus, please proceed, and please consider my guidance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will do. For the information of the Court, this document is part of the Prosecution's first bar table motion. It's number 329 in the bar table motion which was filed on 23rd of November, 2009. It was received pursuant to RFA 1382 from the MUP archives in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, now, President Tihic, can you tell us whether you were aware of any other person by the name of Dragan Djordjevic in Bosanski Samac at the time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember now. I've already said that in terms of age and name and surname, it could be that person. I know that he had finished high school. I know that when he was appointed brigade commander, that people from the staff of the Army of Republika Srpska complained as to how someone who only had a secondary education could be appointed commander. He also got married in Samac. You can check the records there. He married a local girl, so you can check whether that's the same person. It's a part of the official books there of the register of marriages.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would seek to tender this document, not necessarily based on the witness's testimony only, but based because it was received pursuant to RFA 1328 from the MUP archives from -- from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections in relation to this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we would object to the admission of this document on two reasons, basically two reasons. First, authenticity; second, the speculation the witness has shown to the Court as to the nature of the person mentioned in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where is this speculation, Mr. Knoops?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, I think after Your Honours instructed Prosecution to be more clear in -- in delivering a factual foundation, the witness, I quote, said "It could be that person."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and what did he say before that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: He did say that probably this is it Dragan Djordjevic, a second type of speculation. And he also speculated as to the potential age of this person. He was not able to identify any whereabouts of this person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, again, what was his speculation about the age of this person?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I believe it's in line 12. It's, Your Honours, on line 14 running to 16 on page 53. "Well, approximately, that could be it. He was certainly younger than me. I was born in 1951, and this says 1962, and he must have been ten years younger than me." So, speculative, I would say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether that is speculation or -- I know that it's -- I wouldn't -- I wouldn't, every observation as to a difference of age, call that speculation. If you would say that -- and I think the witness only said that he should have been younger and that looking at the difference of age that he considered this in line with what he observed. So whether that's speculation or not is still to be seen. But let's -- you say -- well, first of all, let's see, this document was bar tabled as well. I don't know whether you have responded already to the bar table submission in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And on the basis of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: We didn't deal with this specifically yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what now is the authenticity issue, because that is apparently for -- is -- is whether it is through this witness or on the basis of the bar table submission, that would be important to know --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... right, right. Your Honour, if I may conclude the first submission as to the speculation. The witness also clearly was not able to recollect whether there were other names with the name Dragan Djordjevic. He said, I simply do not know. So we cannot exclude that he was familiar with another person with the name. He is not absolutely clear as to this question. Furthermore, he wasn't able to give any details as to the person he just mentioned. I remember that he underwent high school. So, all in all, we believe there is no basis for admission of this document, simply because it's far from sure whether we are dealing with the same individual. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say that the document can be admitted only if, through this witness, we could firmly establish that the person is the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Because the Prosecution is assuming that this witness is speaking about this person. And the whole intention of tendering this document is the presumption that the -- there is no doubt as to the identity of this Mr. Dragan Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that a matter of weight, or is that a matter of admissibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Admissibility, Your Honour. Because if we are dealing with a separate person, we are admitting a document under the presumption that we are dealing with the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you consider that this Chamber would look at this document as being about the same person if the witness says that he recognises first name, second name, that he sees some similarity in age, that that would, as such, for the Chamber be sufficient to consider that this has now established, through the introduction of this exhibit, that it is the same person?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Not necessarily, Your Honours. I cannot look into Your Honour's mind. But our submission is that the basis for admission should be that there is no doubt that this witness can identify the person in this document. Secondly, as to the authenticity, the signature, which you find at bottom of the document, is -- is disputed by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's the authenticity matter then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. It is not the signature of our defendant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please respond to this latter -- the first matter -- perhaps we deal with a few -- a few of the other elements. Mr. Tihic, are you familiar with the name of the parents of the person you know as Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know where he was born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you know what is -- where Vranje is located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know where Vranje is, but I don't know anyone from Vranje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But could you tell us where it is? Is that close to Bosanski --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is further away, in the southern part of Serbia. Perhaps it's about 300 or even 400 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From Bosanski Samac, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could I ask the Prosecution to perhaps briefly deal with the matters raised?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The Prosecution is tendering this document primarily based on its authenticity resulting from the provision of the document from the MUP archives in -- in Serbia. So the document was received by the Office of the Prosecutor through an RFA, that is, RFA 1382. So in terms of its authenticity, that -- that is the primary basis for its authenticity. As for the witness commenting on it, the witness can only give as much as he can give. And he can only confirm what he confirm. This is the same name that he has referred to throughout, and, therefore, I wanted to show it to him and see whether he could comment upon it. So the primary basis for our submission of tendering the document into evidence is based on its authenticity as a result of having been received pursuant to an RFA as explained in the bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it your position that every document received through am RFA is, for that purpose, authentic? Or for that reason, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Well, I would say that a receipt of a document pursuant to an RFA from the MUP of Serbia does present very significant indicia of authenticity. But certainly the weight to be given to that document is for the Chamber to determine. Especially in comparison to President Tihic's testimony today, it is up to the Chamber to determine whether or not it is satisfied that this is the same individual that President Tihic has been speaking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes you are moving from admissibility to weight to be given, apparently, encouraged by my previous question. But my question was about authenticity. Now, you say we received it through an RFA and therefore that's -- but you have now heard what Mr. Knoops says about the signature, who says that is not the signature of Mr. Stanisic. Have you paid any attention to that yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the quandary we're finding ourselves in is that according to our understanding the Stanisic Defence did not contest the authenticity of any documents from the first bar table motion. So it seems to me that they've already -- we will definitely check on this again, sir, during the break, with your leave. We will check one more time to make sure. But that is my understanding, that the Defence for Stanisic did not contest the authenticity of these documents, including this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I know it's -- I'm out of turn, but I can perhaps assist with the bar table motion. Our response was -- in a sense, a non-response. We said we cannot respond until the indictment issue has been settled. Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that cover also issues like documents being authentic or not because whether or not bearing a signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, we simply took the position that we couldn't -- or wouldn't -- or were not going to respond to the substance of the documents until the Prosecution particularised the link between the documents and a more particularised indictment. I simply stand up to say that it is not correct that we've taken the position that all the documents are authentic. We simply haven't taken a position one way or another in the bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a further look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document will be MFI'd. The Chamber will further consider how to proceed. That is, whether we would require a proof of authenticity or not, whether the link with the witness is good enough. We'll further consider admission in all its aspects. Madam Registrar, the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P179, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'm looking at the clock. We need a break. Ms. Marcus, could you give us an indication as where you are in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would say I would need approximately another 20 minutes, maximum 30. I will try and keep it as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you will go well beyond the two hours you have asked for. So you are encouraged to -- to try to stay within the two hours of your estimate, and to the extent you're not able to do so, to not go much more beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, before we take the break, we return into open session. We are still in closed session. Do we have to remain in closed session after the break?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We will have a break and resume at ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document that was MFI'd during private session should have the status of a confidential document, not a public document, even though it's just MFI'd, nevertheless, we have to give it that status. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: President Tihic, you mentioned in your evidence, your prior evidence, and also you mentioned today some other nicknames in addition to Crni. You mentioned someone called Lugar. You mentioned someone called Beli. You mentioned Zvezdan. Can you tell us, were these individuals members of the same unit or of different units, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: They acted together. They were the special forces, as we called them. Whether they were a single unit or whether they comprised several units which were merged, that is something I don't know. But it was a joint team, so to say, commanded by Djordjevic, aka Crni.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, earlier today, you mentioned the name of Zvezdan Jovanovic it was in the -- it was not reflected in the transcript, but I think it was at page 35, line 23, to page 36, line 2, of the temporary transcript. You also mentioned this name in your Milosevic testimony a few times. Could you tell us who was this person, Zvezdan Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Zvezdan Jovanovic, the public knows this person as the assassin of Zoran Djindjic, the prime-minister of Serbia. I met him during my stay in the Samac camp. He beat me as well. After a number of years when I saw his photographs -- photograph in the daily press in Bosnia-Herzegovina under which it said the Serbian PM assassin, I recognised him immediately. I discussed it with some friends of mine who were in Samac at the time, be it in the camp itself or outside, and they all agreed with me that the person in the photograph is Zvezdan Jovanovic who was in Samac as one of the special forces members. A cousin of mine who was not detained and who used to know Zvezdan because they associated, remembers Jovanovic telling him, Oh, by the way, last night I beat up your cousin. And stuff like that. I called him and he confirmed to me that indeed this that was Zvezdan Jovanovic. In Samac he was the master of life and death.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Apart from the beatings that you sustained at the hands of this Zvezdan Jovanovic, did you witness any other crimes committed in Bosanski Samac by Zvezdan Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I know, from what others said, that he was a criminal. He seized vehicles. And I know a person he used who worked in the administration who would change registration papers of those cases -- cars so that he could sell them in Serbia later on. I saw him around as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: President Tihic, I'm going to show you a very short clip from a video in which members of the special operations unit of the Republic of Serbia state security are being introduced to Slobodan Milosevic. I'm going to ask our Case Manager, Mr. Laugel, to play the clip for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P61.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Mr. President, veterans of the Special Operations Unit of the Republic of Serbia State Security are lined up for inspection. Colonel Zika Ivanovic reporting. "Hello, Ivanovic. "Mr. President, allow me to introduce the unit's veteran officers. " Mr. President, Colonel Radojica Bozovic. " Hello, Bozovic, I read those reports of yours. " Thank you ... God forbid there should be more of them, but should there be, I'm here. " Colonel Dusan Orlovic. " Pleased to meet you. " Likewise, comrade president. " Colonel Vasilije Miojovic. " Pleased to meet you. " Colonel Goran Opacic. " Hello. " Colonel Predrag Prica. " Pleased to meet you. " Lieutenant-Colonel Zvezdan Jovanovic. " Pleased to meet you. " Lieutenant-Colonel Sirno Ratkovic. " Pleased to meet you. " Lieutenant-Colonel, pilot, Milutin Radivojevic. " Pleased to meet you. " Good. " Major Nikola Filipovic. " Hello, major. " Major Davor Subotic. " Hello. " Major Miroljub Budimir. " Hello. " Captain, Doctor, Miroljub Savic. " Hello. " Captain Dragan Oljuic. " Hello. " Captain Dragisa Grujic. " Pleased to meet you. " Captain Dragoljub Ratkovic. " Pleased to meet you. " Captain Nikola Loncar. " Pleased to meet you. Welcome. " Captain Djurica Banjac. " Hello. " Captain Dragoljub Popovic. " Hello. " Lieutenant Svetozar Nakarada. " Hello Svetozar."

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: President Tihic, we have heard a man named Zvezdan Jovanovic being introduced to Mr. Milosevic. Is this the same man as the one whom you describe in your evidence as having been the master of life and death?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: This footage is not perfectly clear, but I'd say this is the person. The footage is a bit dark, but the build is the same, although I cannot see his eyes or face clearly. But I think Zvezdan Jovanovic is this person. That person did what he did later on, and people of Bosanski Samac know him. I'm not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up 65 ter 3679. I'm sorry, I'm sorry -- no, no, in fact -- that's correct, I'm slightly dyslexic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: President Tihic, can you tell us what we're looking at in this photo, in these photos?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: You can see two houses. It used to be by me and my brother. We used it as business premises and part of -- of which was my legal office. You can see what is left of the inscription that was there. They burned it at the outset, the first or the second day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was written there before it was destroyed. Can you read to us what is written there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It says, attorney-at-law, Sulejman Tihic. Because, at that time, I was a lawyer, and this was my office, across the street from the court building.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I now ask the Court Officer, please, to call up 65 ter 3769. And the English on -- yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: President Tihic, do you have personal knowledge of the contents of this document?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I see from the text that all persons are refused leave to leave the territory of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac without passes. This order was in place, and no one could leave Samac without their approval.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How did this impact upon the community in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It had a negative impact, in the sense that people felt helpless, fearful. Those citizens who remained and who were not Serbs were later used in exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. Did you want to add something, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: And they were constantly exposed to attacks, maltreatment, rapes, thefts. Those of us who stayed, who were unable to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence. It's not one of the related exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any objections? I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P180, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P180 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: President Tihic, that document that we just saw, which -- which restricted freedom of movement for non-Serbs in Bosanski Samac, was this policy part of what you referred to earlier today as the political project?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: The restriction of movement served primarily to retain a portion of the population who were Muslims and Croats, in order to have people for exchanges, who could be exchanged for the Serbs who were on the other side and who had been detained or captured. The ultimate goal was for all of them to leave the area finally, to move out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, you refer to the document as the document which restricted freedom of movement for non-Serbs. Was the document talking about all persons or about non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Perhaps I should put the question to President Tihic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm asking what the document says. So, therefore, let's look at the document. It disappeared from my screen, but ... I don't see any -- any restriction in the document. Apart from how it was used, how it was practiced, but you refer to the document as the document which limited the freedom of movement on non-Serbs. And I think, as a matter of fact, that the document talks about no individual without any reference to ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You are correct, Your Honours, and it was -- I was referring back to the comment by President Tihic as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But could you please clearly distinguish between -- well, and even in the testimony of Mr. Tihic, I don't think that he said that this was -- he said that those citizens who remained and who were not Serbs were later used in exchanges. That is non-Serbs, apparently, who were subject to this rule were exchanged. It doesn't say -- even the testimony in that respect doesn't say how it was specifically applied to the various ethnicities. May I ask you to be very precise in referring to documents. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: A final question for you, President Tihic. Can you tell the Court how your prior experiences have affected you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Irrespective of everything that had taken place, even at such times you could come across what I would say humans and non-humans. Even after all this, people will go on living together in Bosnia-Herzegovina; Croats, Serbs, and Muslims, because it's a society of that type, despite the conflicts and suffering. The project, which was aimed at separating the peoples and which aimed at arousing conflict, failed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes the examination-in-chief, but I am prepared to make a brief submission in relation to Your Honours' original query as to the quantity of documents being tendered and the quantity of prior statements and transcripts. I could make it now; I could make it after the close of the cross-examination; or in written submissions, as Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would prefer if, at this moment, we would further hear the evidence of the witness and delay that other matter. And we'll consider what's the most appropriate way in dealing with it. It could be that if we have time that we invite you to do it orally, and if no time remains, we might ask written submissions for that purpose. The sequence of cross-examination. Mr. Knoops, you will be first the first one to ... So it is the Stanisic Defence who will start to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Tihic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Knoops. Mr. Knoops is counsel for Mr. Stanisic. Please proceed, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tihic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: [In English] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I will try to follow the line of questioning my learned friend of the Prosecution has followed, so I'd first like to start with some of your background information, if you don't mind. Sir, is it correct that you never served in the military?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: For health reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. So, it's fair to say that you have no knowledge on military structures of command and control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I know about the military structure, to the extent of what I was familiar with as a lawyer. But in terms of command, no, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: But as a lawyer, were you involved in military cases?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So it's fair to say that what you have testified about, in terms of your observations, in terms of who's commanding individuals, is purely based on your subjective feeling; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I base that on what I could see, on what I felt, and on the things I discussed with others or learned through conversations with others. People did not introduce themselves to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. But if you had to describe in those days, in April 1992, the military structure of the JNA, were you able to set up a structure?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army was representative through the Ministry of Defence in the federal government. In terms of command, at the top there was the General Staff, then Military Districts, corps, brigades, detachments, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And this is based on your knowledge through other sources; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: My knowledge is similar to the knowledge of any person who dealt with politics, and the structure of the JNA was part of the legal system. I knew the basic legislation pertaining to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: But it's correct that if it would come to details how a military unit would operate, you would have no knowledge, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: How they operated. I know the basic things like others. The principle of subordination and command, superior/subordinate relationship. That's what I know specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tihic. You introduced today, again, the name of Mr. Simic. Could you give us a brief description of Mr. Simic? Let me be very specific: Is it correct that he was part of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps learned counsel could specify which Simic he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Blagoje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is about Blagoje Simic and whether he was part of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blagoje Simic was the president of the SDS and deputy speaker of the legally elected Municipal Assembly in Bosanski Samac. After that, he was president of the Serb municipality of Bosanski Samac. I knew him before the war, I knew his brother, his father, if that's what you want to note.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the other microphones be switched off while the witness is answering. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He also commanded the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Mr. Tihic, that he was a hard-liner in terms of a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Maybe we can pull up Exhibit P180; Prosecution document just shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, you have in front again before you document P180. Could you explain to the Court who issued this document?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It says the Crisis Staff of the municipality. I can suppose, although I don't see the first and last name and I don't recognise the signature, but I assume it was signed by the president of the Crisis Staff. The president was Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that it is likely that this document was issued by Blagoje Simic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It is likely. Although it -- his name is not there. But it is only logical that the president signed Crisis Staff documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you testified that you were privy to some of the conversations with Mr. Simic. Is it correct, sir, that he actually enforced these kinds of decisions without approval of anyone?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know how he enforced these decisions. At that time, I was detained. On the 21st of May, I was already in Batajnica in the military prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you have a look at Article 2 of that decision, mentioning the public security station. You see that? Yes. Have you any idea why it's --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Have you any idea why the public security station is mentioned here in Article 2?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: The public security station is in charge of civilians, and the military command was in charge of conscripts. That's why I believe this is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. At the bottom of this document you see that it is copied to the public security station as well as military commands. My question is: Do you know what military commands are referred to here, or meant?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I can presume again. This is the 21st of May. I think it has to do with certain military commands of the Serb TO or the armed forces, the commands which existed in the field at the time. I suppose these were local commands, because the Municipal Crisis Staff could not issue orders to larger military formations. I can only guess, but it would be illogical for a Municipal Crisis Staff to issue orders to senior commands. They presumably could do so in the case of local units, such as the Territorial Defence Staff of Samac, and the units -- Serb units which were under that staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that this document is actually an order to the military command? Apart from whether it was a bigger unit or a smaller unit. It is directed to the military command. Is that a fair reading of the document, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: That's what it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: -- but there's no logic in a municipal level issuing orders to commands of Military Districts, corps, or brigades. I think this had to do with the local population which was organised as part of the Serb TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Tihic, do you agree with me that at that time it was not uncommon for a Crisis Staff to issuing orders to military commanders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't think a Crisis Staff could issue orders to military commands. Military commands were senior to Crisis Staffs in my assessment. And I mean the Crisis Staffs of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yeah, but we're not dealing with ordinary situations, sir, we're dealing with a state of emergency. Is it correct, that, in the state of emergency, the Crisis Staff was empowered to issue orders to military units?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. Military structures issue orders to military units. They can only issue orders to local military units that are within a Territorial Defence Staff, whereas, the others get orders from the minister, from their commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: But this is your assumption. You just testified that you have no knowledge on military structures. But can you exclude the possibility that this order was issued from the Crisis Staff, i.e., Mr. Simic, to the local military command, at that time present in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, the witness cannot exclude that on the basis of his previous testimony, I can answer the question. The witness has said, in many respects, that he has to guess; he doesn't know precisely this and this and this; and then to say, Can you exclude ... I could answer that question for him. The witness, apparently -- you can ask him what he knows. You earlier objected against seeking opinion. You will ask five, six, or seven questions, we're all seeking opinion not with a proper factual basis. The only question which was really of a factual character was the question whether it was common at the time that a certain thing happened. The witness did not answer that question. Let's -- let's try to get -- Mr. Tihic, when did you see this document for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, perhaps. I don't know. During this session or during proofing. Perhaps this was one of the documents that was shown to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, do you have any knowledge of -- you said earlier that you were in prison. Do you have any knowledge gained in whatever way about who were addressed, how it was distributed, how it was enforced? Do you have any factual knowledge of -- of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no factual knowledge. I can just assume how things may function, you see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, you see, a military unit is rather -- or, rather, it functions at a far broader level than a municipality. And now if every municipal staff were to issue orders to that military unit that pertains to ten municipalities, there is no logic. These order can be different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you already told us a couple of times of what you considered to be logic and not. Now sometimes facts are not always in accordance with logic. Sometimes they are, sometimes they are not. Mr. Knoops, we've heard a lot of logic and conclusions. And if you don't -- if have you no idea about in which way this was distributed, to whom it was addressed, whether it's logic, et cetera, et cetera, to address it to A, B, or C, then, of course, with that level of knowledge of what happened, you can't exclude anything. Therefore, I think that question is answered, although not by the witness but by me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, it's correct that Mr. Blagoje Simic made the proposal to divide -- to make the division of the Serbs from the non-Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And is it correct that he would threaten you and your colleagues in that time with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: He did not say it specifically, but he said that, unless he got an answer, a positive answer, a favourable answer within seven day, he knows in which way to achieve --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the rest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did not say whether he would do it through the JNA or in some other way, but we took it as a threat of use of force.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off while the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: May I please ask the Court Usher to pull up P174, please. It's page 2, the English version, fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And it reads in line 7 -- sorry, 9. Line 9. Mr. Tihic, you have before the B/C/S version of your statement of 28 February 1995, page 2, fourth paragraph, line 9, saying: "Every time I had some private contact with him," referring to Blagoje Simic, "he would threaten us with the JNA." Do you see it sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: The paragraph starts with -- after four days before the attack -- sorry. About four days after the attack, I believe it was the Monday before, the Serbs insisted on having a meeting of municipality representatives, et cetera. You see that paragraph, sir. Yeah?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't see that. But I remember that I have already spoken about that. Maybe you could scroll back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There we are. I think have now the right page in front of us. The first long paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Tihic, you say, in 1995: "Every time I had some private contact with him, he would threaten us with the JNA?" Do you remember that statement, sir? Is it a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It is correct. Whatever is written there is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me about a specific date, just before the attack? You asked me whether he threatened with the JNA on that day by presenting an ultimatum to us a few days before the attack when he was asking for a Serb municipality of Samac. That is how I understood your question. Whether he then made threats concerning the JNA. He did not mention the JNA on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Doesn't matter. So -- but he did threaten with the JNA, irrespective of the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I understood your question to pertain to that specific meeting, and that is why I gave the answer I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to be unclear. But -- so, Mr. Simic threatened you in the days before the attack with JNA. Is that correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what is written here, that that's what I said, that he then made threats involving the JNA. We didn't know of anybody else's existence then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you not to elaborate on what you think. Just please stick to the question. Mr. Simic did threaten you with the JNA. What do you refer -- what you mean with the wording "every time."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, look, if we're going to see what I said with full authenticity, he said that the Serbs have the support of the JNA. There is a difference there. Isn't there? He didn't say the JNA would do that. He said that he had the support of the JNA. And that can mean providing them with weapons, securing logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, is it correct that --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, that Mr. Simic threatened to say, If you are not agreeing with the proposal, I will call in the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No, no, he did not say that he would call the JNA. He didn't say that. He said that he knew a way in which he could resolve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And is it correct that he threatened you and the people who were with you at that time to get support from the JNA, in terms of weapons, logistics, forces, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Not on that day. On that day he did not mention the JNA or support or anything else, but he did say that he knew in which way he would achieve that. He didn't mention anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And on how many occasions did he elaborate on this JNA involvement?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, Blagoje Simic spoke less about the JNA. It was Simo Zaric who spoke more of the JNA and Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic and this Fourth Detachment. He generally spoke about the general support of the JNA. The Serbs have the support of the JNA. And the representatives of the JNA were Simo Zaric, Radovan Antic who were in the structures there. They spoke about the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it correct that Zaric was also a member of the SDS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No. No. Zaric was the League of Communists, the Socialist Party, whatever; he was never SDS. They didn't like him. His wife was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did you, at any time, notice that Mr. Simic did speak to Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic about the support of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he did speak. But as a rule, Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic came to meetings with Simo Zaric and Radovan Antic. Those were the persons that Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic relied on in Bosanski Samac, at least at the meetings that I attended. And it was Simo Zaric more than Antic. And they were the commander and assistant commander of that Fourth Detachment of theirs in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that the decision to attack came from Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who it was that took the decision to attack. I can just guess, on the basis of other sources. But I don't know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last part of your answer. You said: But I don't know ... and what did you then say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who specifically made the decision to attack Samac. I can just guess, on the basis of the information that I have. It wasn't Nikolic. That's it. Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic was not the one who did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Could we please pull up P173. Referring to page 5 of the statement of the witness in -- in English version, starting with the paragraph reading: "The night before Samac was attacked, Bozanovic Fitozovic, Simo Zaric and the presidents of all the parties had a meeting to decide ..." et cetera. I ask the witness to look at that paragraph, in specific the 14th sentence -- 14th line starting with: "I think the decision to attack came from Nikolic" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first get the right page in B/C/S on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6 in B/C/S, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Witness? The paragraph in which it's mentioned, 14th line: "I think the decision to attack came from Nikolic in Brcko, but I don't know who gave Nikolic the order."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I can't find that. "I think the decision to attack came from Nikolic in Brcko, but I do not know who gave Nikolic the order. It could be ..." I said I think. However, later, on the basis of some information that I received --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: My question is -- my question is --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't think it came from Nikolic. I think that Nikolic was also taken by surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: But on what basis you stated in 1995 that you thought that decision to attack came from Nikolic? What was the basis of the information which led to you think that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, in 1995, the war was still under way. And now, after the war, just look at Simo Zaric's book. Read it. And you will see from whom the attack -- the order to attack came from. He was taken by surprise too. Some other information showed that the army got involved in the attack on Samac, only several hours after these other units, the special units, and the Territorial Defence Staff of Republika Srpska entered the town. I said that, because that's what I thought at the time. In the mean time, I hadn't had any contact with some people out there in the field. Hadn't seen them in quite a while. And then I came to realise that what I had thought at the time was not correct, that the order had come from another side, not down the military line. That is clearly stated in Simo Zaric's book. You can buy the book. He was involved in the Simic/Zaric case, and he explains that very specifically where the attack came -- or, rather, where the attack order came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I have to interrupt. So you are saying that on the basis of a book you're now withdrawing your statement from 1994 in which you informed the investigators of the Prosecution that you, at that time, were of the opinion that a decision to attack came from Nikolic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I'm not withdrawing my statement. You see that I said then "I think" and so on. I didn't say I assert. I said I think. On the basis of what I had available at that point in time. To think and to assert are two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: We leave that point for now. We go page 4 of your statement of 1994 which, in the second paragraph of the English version, states -- if you please have a look at it, the English version, page 4, second paragraph starting with: "The Territorial Defence was not made up of professional soldiers ..." et cetera. The last line of that paragraph reads: "I do not personally know from where Nikolic got his orders, but only the military command in Belgrade could give orders or have authority over the JNA." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I can't see that. But it is only logical that Nikolic can get his orders from the command up there in Belgrade. Of course. I mean, the page hasn't opened yet, so I can't see what is written there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we always try to find the version that the witness can read. I think it is -- Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 4 in B/C/S. The last lines on page 4 and the very beginning of page 5 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think the -- I think Mr. Knoops specifically referred to the last part of that paragraph which is on the next page. Could you please take your time to read the first paragraph as it appears on your screen now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it. I have said that I personally do not know where Nikolic got his orders from but it was only the military command in Belgrade that could give orders and have authority over the JNA. That is a general statement, a general position, on the basis of the knowledge that I had. As I said a few moments ago, what I know about the military structure, that superiors give orders to their subordinates. So it's only logical that Nikolic who was in Brcko gets his orders from someone above him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I didn't yet pose a question to you. Would you please wait for the question and not elaborate on logic or illogical things, please, sir. Now my question is: Do you agree with me that you're not speaking here of thinking but you are specifically referring to Nikolic getting his orders which is a different thing from that you thought that he was involved in the attack; is that correct? You, in other words, don't -- you do not make any reservation here except that you don't personally know it, but you say --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It's the most important thing there. I'm saying I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Okay. Not going to discuss this point. I'm putting to you that Mr. Simic called in the JNA through Nikolic to attack Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No. No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: There's a difference between no, and I don't think so, I believe. So what is it? You don't know, or you --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: No. No. No. Simic cannot call Nikolic to attack Samac, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So let's -- let's try to get -- let's try to get matters straight. You say you do not know from whom Nikolic got his orders. Secondly, you say it would not be very logic that he would have received his orders from Simic. That's your answer. I agree with Mr. Knoops, and I said before, logic is -- is not -- I can imagine that you describe that, but we -- you are a witness of fact and you say, I do not know from whom he got his orders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: If you don't know, did you see, at that time -- point in time, any documents indicating how exactly Mr. Simic was communicating with any other individuals or politicians?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Documents? Whether I saw any document? I don't remember. Perhaps if you have some document that I could comment upon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: We are not putting, yet, a document to you. I put to you that the attack on Bosanski Samac was effected by the 7th [sic] Corps of the JNA that belonged to the 2nd Military District in cooperation with the local authorities, i.e., Mr. Simic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: It's not correct, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: The transcript reads "7th Corps." It's "17th Corps," sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Witness, that the local authorities of Bosanski Samac had, at that time, intensive communications with the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, and this may be my last question, Your Honour, for this topic, then we could potentially adjourn. In your statement of 1995, which is P174, page 3, English version, page 3, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's always wait until we have the document in both languages on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: It's the seventh paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: You find it, Mr. Witness? You see it? Starting with the line: "I consider the following people to be the most responsible for the planning of" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we wait until we have the document -- now we have it. And, as a matter of fact, not the right page yet, as far as I can see. No, it's still not -- there we are. Do you see it at the bottom of the page in your own language? Please proceed, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, you see, there, the paragraph starting with the words: "I consider the following people to be the most responsible for the planing of and executing the attack on Bosanski Samac." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Could you read, please, the first name, the first names?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: Simo Zaric and Blagoje Simic. Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic, Captain Petrovic, chief of KOS for the attack on the town, Radovan Antic and Mirko Jovanovic, Stevo Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: That will do, witness. Sorry. Just the first line. So you -- so you agree with me that you blame Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic, Simic, Zaric, Petrovic, chief of KOS, for the planning of and the execution of the attack. Did you -- do you still stand to this statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC
utterances.text: According to the information I had then, I made that statement then. They all did take part in the attack on Samac, after all. Especially, well, both Zaric and Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Thank you, Mr. Witness. We will deal with the separate names later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, if I may suggest, to finish this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I inquire with you, Mr. Knoops, and with the other parties on the timing of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Sorry? I had my microphone off. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would inquire with the parties how much time they think they would need for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I would, say from the Stanisic Defence, maximum one hour left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One hour left. And the Simatovic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that it will be one hour, perhaps a bit more than one hour. Of course, it depends on the questions that my colleague will put. But I believe that one hour would be an optimum and the most realistic from our point of view. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking which would mean that we would start the next witness tomorrow, somewhere in the second session, most likely, possibly at the beginning of the third session. If the parties would please keep that in mind that -- and it also is clear that, for planning purposes, it's also important to know whether the next witness has to remain stand by or not. So that's one of the reasons why I'm asking. Mr. Tihic, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak or in any other way communicate with anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony you have given already today, or whether that's testimony still to be given tomorrow. We would like to see you back tomorrow, at a quarter past 2.00, because we adjourn. And we'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 4th of February, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of February, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.
